Recommendation: Protect the top revenue decile before chasing new customers
Evidence: The top 20% of customers produce 64.33% of revenue and the top 10% produce 45.39%. Losing a handful of them costs more than a month of acquisition.
Suggested_Action: Give the top decile a named owner and review them monthly on the Customer Intelligence page, sorted by revenue with recency visible.

Recommendation: Contact the 52 high-value customers who have not bought for 180+ days
Evidence: 52 customers are flagged potentially at risk: high historical value and no delivered order for at least 180 days at the 2026-01-01 reference date. Their lifetime revenue is ₹26.51 L and their estimated next-12-month profit is ₹2.15 L.
Suggested_Action: Work the list from the Customer Segmentation page (filter Potentially_At_Risk_High_Value = 1) and record the outcome; this is an inactivity flag, not a confirmed loss.

Recommendation: Convert single-purchase buyers: they are 10.6% of customers but 1.4% of revenue
Evidence: Repeat customers (89.42% of the base) generate 98.59% of revenue, at ₹33,378 each against ₹4,019 for single-purchase customers.
Suggested_Action: Target the second order specifically: the median gap between repeat purchases is 54 days (BQ17), so a follow-up inside two months is the natural window.
Supporting_Metric: Revenue per repeat customer vs single-purchase

Recommendation: Treat Champions as a retention job, not an acquisition one
Evidence: Champions are 16.84% of customers and 53.83% of revenue, with average recency 33 days. The K-Means 'High-Value, Active' cluster tells the same story from unsupervised features (55.67% of revenue).
Suggested_Action: Monitor Champions' recency monthly on the Customer Segmentation page; a rise in average recency inside this segment is an early warning that outweighs a good total-revenue month.

Recommendation: Stop judging Electronics on revenue alone
Evidence: Electronics is 50.10% of revenue but only 23.29% of profit, at a 10.85% margin. Beauty and Fashion earn 46.49% and 42.77%.
Suggested_Action: Report Electronics with revenue and margin side by side (Product Analytics page) and set category targets on profit, not turnover.
Supporting_Metric: Electronics revenue share vs profit share

Recommendation: Review the 10 products the margin and returns rules flag
Evidence: The flagged products fall into two groups: high-revenue items whose margin is under half their category's (Nova X7 Pro Smartphone 256GB, AeroBook Pro 16 Laptop, 43-inch 4K Smart TV), and Fashion items whose return/cancel rate is more than 1.5x the overall rate.
Suggested_Action: Take one decision per flagged product - reprice, renegotiate cost, or accept it as a traffic driver - and record which; the Product Analytics scatter shows revenue against profit so a loss-making high-revenue product cannot hide.

Recommendation: Treat discounting as a margin decision, not a volume lever
Evidence: Within categories, the 0% discount band has the highest margin in 6 of 6 categories, and overall margin falls from 29.31% at 0% to 20.43% in the 31-40% band. In Electronics the 21-40% band is margin-negative (BQ08).
Suggested_Action: Cap discounts in low-margin categories and approve deep discounts case by case. This is an association in observational data, not proof that discounting causes the loss - the products that get discounted may differ systematically.
Supporting_Metric: Categories where the 0% band has the best margin

Recommendation: Attack Fashion returns: 14.44% of booked value is lost
Evidence: Fashion loses 14.44% of booked value to returns and cancellations (₹20.36 L), against 9.43% company-wide. Its returned-line rate is 10.94%.
Suggested_Action: Work on sizing information and product photography for the Fashion sub-categories with the highest return rates; every point recovered lands on the company's second-best margin.

Recommendation: Grow Central and East on their margin, not on their size
Evidence: Central and East are the two smallest regions (12.71% and 12.39% of revenue) but carry the two highest margins (25.26% and 24.78%), while South leads revenue at 27.02% on a 22.80% margin.
Suggested_Action: Test incremental spend in Central and East where each rupee of revenue currently carries more profit, and use the Regional Analytics page to watch whether margin holds as volume grows.

Recommendation: Do not build a region-specific pricing story - the differences are category mix
Evidence: No region-category pair sits more than 2 percentage points below the national margin for that category (BQ16), so regional margin gaps come from what each region buys, not from how it is served.
Suggested_Action: Read regional margin through the region x category matrix on the Regional Analytics page before concluding that a region is underperforming.
Supporting_Metric: Region-category pairs more than 2pp below national margin

Recommendation: Route the customer-level actions by region, because value concentration is not uniform
Evidence: Revenue per customer ranges from ₹28,394 to ₹32,434 across regions, and AOV from ₹4,723 to ₹5,108.
Suggested_Action: Use the Region slicer with the customer pages so retention effort is sized to where the high-value customers actually sit.
Supporting_Metric: Revenue per customer, highest vs lowest region

Recommendation: Plan capacity around the October-December peak
Evidence: October is the highest-revenue month in all three years and the top three months by average revenue are October, November, December; October alone carries 12.9% of an average year's revenue.
Suggested_Action: Set inventory, staffing and campaign budgets against the monthly profile on the Revenue Intelligence page rather than a flat monthly average.
Supporting_Metric: October share of an average year

Evidence: Revenue grew 51.37% in 2024 and 37.72% in 2025, and margin rose across the same years (22.65% -> 23.90%).
Suggested_Action: Track revenue growth % and margin on the same page every month; growth bought by margin is visible immediately on the Revenue Intelligence page.

Recommendation: Recover part of the 9.43% of booked value lost to returns and cancellations
Evidence: ₹6.63 Cr was booked and ₹6.01 Cr was delivered; ₹0.63 Cr never became revenue. Cash on delivery has the highest cancellation rate (6.19% of lines against 3.66% for UPI).
Suggested_Action: Add an order-confirmation step for high-value COD orders and measure the cancelled-line rate by payment method after the change.

Recommendation: Plan the next two quarters on ₹1.58 Cr of forecast revenue, with the interval shown
Evidence: The Step 9 Theta model forecasts ₹1.58 Cr for 2026-01 to 2026-06, with an 80% interval of ₹1.00 Cr to ₹2.16 Cr. The previous six months delivered ₹1.50 Cr.
Suggested_Action: Budget to the central forecast, stress-test to the lower bound, and re-fit the model as each actual month lands - the interval widens with horizon, so month 6 is not month 1.

Recommendation: Trust the monthly forecast at about ±7.8% and no further
Evidence: On the held-out test months the forecast's MAPE was 7.77% (MAE ₹2.13 L), and the mean rolling-backtest MAPE was 14.56%.
Suggested_Action: Quote the forecast with its error band on the Prediction & Forecast page; do not set targets at a precision the model has never demonstrated.

Recommendation: Use the customer-level revenue prediction for ranking, not for rupee commitments
Evidence: The Step 8 Linear regression reaches R² 0.056 with MAE ₹5,658 per customer-quarter on the test split - better than the best baseline on RMSE, but far from precise for an individual customer. Its total bias is +1.12%.
Suggested_Action: Use the predictions to order customers for outreach (top predicted customers first) and take the aggregate total as a planning figure; never quote a single customer's predicted revenue as a commitment.

Recommendation: Re-run the pipeline before each planning cycle
Evidence: Every figure on this dashboard is a snapshot: RFM, clusters and CLV are taken at the 2026-01-01 reference date and the forecast is fitted on 2023-01 to 2025-12 (36 months).
Suggested_Action: Re-run Steps 3-10 and refresh the extracts (see powerbi_user_guide.md) so segments and forecasts move with the data instead of ageing silently on the page.
